https://www.telegraph.co.uk/world-news/2.title: Drone strikes help Ukraine smash through Russian lines in Kharkiv
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/world-news/2.text:
Ukraine’s Bayraktar armed drones have helped its forces penetrate 50 kilometres into Russian-held territory and recapture more than 20 towns and villages in an ongoing counter-offensive.
Brigadier General Oleksiy Gromov hailed the Turkish-made drones as he gave details on Ukraine’s counter-offensive on Thursday.
"Enemy infantry and motorised artillery units unprotected by air defence systems become easy prey for our Bayraktars, the quantity of which is always increasing, thanks to our volunteers," he said, referring to international fund-raising campaigns to buy more of the drones for Ukraine.
More than 700 sq km of land has been brought under Ukrainian control, he said, while Ukrainian troops in Kherson also made significant gains and “advanced deep into the Russian defences”.
US Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin earlier on Thursday said President Joe Biden had approved a $675 million weapons package for Ukraine, as he and other defence ministers met in Germany to discuss how to continue supporting Kyiv in the long-term.
Activists from environmental group Greenpeace blocked a shipment of Russian gas from unloading at a terminal in Sweden on Thursday.
"Activists climbed up on the loading arms at the terminal and they have boats in the water", a spokeswoman for terminal owner Gasum, Olga Vaisanen, told AFP.
She said the protest at the Nynashamn terminal near Stockholm began in the morning and lasted for more than five hours, though police eventually forced the activists to climb down from the loading arms.
Greenpeace's sailboat Witness and activists in kayaks were blocking the Dutch-registered LNG tanker Coral Energy from docking and unloading.
The activists demanded the Swedish government immediately halt its imports of Russian gas.
"That Russian gas is still allowed to flow into Sweden, more than six months after Putin began his bloody invasion of Ukraine, is unacceptable", Greenpeace campaigner Karolina Carlsson said in a statement.
There are currently no EU or Swedish sanctions on gas imports from Russia, only on oil and coal.
The United States sees no indication that a UN-brokered Ukrainian grain export deal is unravelling, the White House said on Thursday, after President Vladimir Putin triggered fears that Russia could withdraw support.
"We see no indication that it's falling apart now and it is in fact having the intended effect," White House national security spokesman John Kirby told reporters.
Ukrainian forces are making "clear and real progress" on the battlefield against Russia, US Secretary of State Antony Blinken has said on a visit to Kyiv.
"It's very early, but we are seeing clear and real progress on the ground, particularly in the area around Kherson, but also some interesting developments in the Donbas in the east," Mr Blinken told reporters.
Mr Blinken, who met President Volodymyr Zelensky, said that he saw a "real effectiveness" in the counter-offensive launched by Ukraine.
"We are proud of the fact that our support and the support of so many other countries is helping to enable what the Ukrainians are doing – working to liberate territory seized by Russia in this aggression," he said.
With over 5 million downloads, our Ukraine: The Latest podcast is your go-to source for all the latest analysis, live reaction and correspondents reporting on the ground.
Today, David Knowles (Host) and Dom Nicholls (Associate Editor, Defence) discuss the latest updates the battlefront and we have a fascinating interview with Vladyslav Heraskevych, the first-ever Ukrainian skeleton racer, who talks about how the war has impacted Sport in Ukraine and his own life.
Russia has threatened to retaliate against European Union curbs on visas for Russians, but said it would not close itself off from the bloc.
"The interests of us, of our people, will be taken into account in the first place when choosing retaliatory measures," Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told reporters on Thursday.
"The Russian Federation won't close itself up to the EU in response," she said.
Ukrainian forces have broken through Russian lines with a "tank fist" as they advanced 12 miles on a lightning offensive in Kharkiv region, writes Roland Oliphant.
The Ukrainian military continued to maintain an official silence about the progress of the battle south of Kharkiv, but multiple unofficial sources on both sides indicated that Ukrainian forces were trying to reach the strategic junction of Kupiansk.
That would leave thousands of Russian troops based in Izyum trapped against the Oskol river, a tributary of the Siversky Donets, with only three vulnerable bridges across which to evacuate.
Read the full story by Roland Oliphant here
Ukraine has struck over 400 Russian targets with HIMARS rocket systems, General Mark Milley, the Chairman of the US Joint Chiefs of Staff, has said.
"We are seeing real and measurable gains from Ukraine in the use of these systems. For example, the Ukrainians have struck over 400 targets with the HIMARS and they've had devastating effect", he told reporters at Ramstein air base.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that US Secretary of State Antony Blinken's visit to Kyiv sent an important signal to Ukraine as it pressed a counter-offensive against Russia in the south and east.
"This is a very important signal that the United States is with us. For us this is a guarantee that we can return our territories and our land," Mr Zelensky said in video comments on Thursday.
Norway will donate about 160 Hellfire missiles to Ukraine, its defence ministry has announced.
Ukrainian troops have reportedly already been trained to use the missiles by Norwegian instructors.
The Hellfire missile is an advanced anti-tank weapon that is usually fired from helicopters or drones but can also be launched from land-based platforms.
Norway will also donate night vision equipment for Ukraine's armed forces.

A "political" cap on gas imports from Russia only would not help bring down energy prices for European households and businesses, Belgium's Energy Minister Tinne Van der Straeten told Reuters ahead of emergency EU talks on Friday.
The price cap on Russian pipeline gas imports, proposed by the EU executive ahead of Friday's ministerial talks aimed at lowering runaway energy prices, has so far met a mixed reception in the bloc's 27 nations.
"Our intention first and foremost is to bring prices down. A cap on only Russian gas won't bring prices down," she said. "A cap on just Russian gas is purely political."
Instead, Belgium wants an EU-wide, dynamic price cap on exchange traded gas that is linked to Asian markets, something Ms Van der Straeten said would ensure safety of supplies.
Ukrainian troops have recaptured more than 700 square km of territory in the south and in the eastern Kharkiv region, where they advanced up to 50 km into Russian lines and retook more than 20 villages, a Ukrainian general has said.
Brigadier General Oleksiy Gromov gave the most detailed public assessment so far of Ukraine's counter-offensive on Thursday. Kyiv has so far declined to disclose many details so as not to compromise the operation.
"During defence operations to recapture lost territory in the Kharkiv direction, since the start of the week, Ukraine's armed forces... have penetrated into enemy's lines by a depth of up to 50 km," Brig Gen Gromov said.
"Enemy infantry and motorized artillery units unprotected by air defence systems become easy prey for our Bayraktars, the quantity of which is always increasing, thanks to our volunteers," he said, referring to Ukraine's fleet of Turkish-made armed drones.
Poland has joined the Baltic states in limiting the admission of Russian nationals on its territory.
Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia this week agreed to limit the entry of Russian nationals into their countries from Russia and Belarus.
"It is unacceptable that, while people in Ukraine are being tortured and murdered, citizens from the aggressor state (Russia) can travel freely within the EU," the Polish government said in a statement, adding the new measures should enter into force by September 19.
"The measures are adopted on the basis of the common rationale of the protection of public order and internal security, as well as the overall security of our common Schengen area," the government said.
Germany and the Netherlands will train Ukrainian soldiers in how to detect and clear mines and booby traps, their defence ministers have said.
German Defense Minister Christine Lambrecht and her Dutch counterpart Kajsa Ollongren announced the plan in a news conference at the US military base in Ramstein.
The training will be given at the explosive ordnance defense school in Stetten am Kalten Markt, in Germany’s south-west, Ms Lambrecht said.
"We will not only provide the training, but also the material," she said, adding that the facility is able to train around 20 Ukrainian soldiers. "It will be able to happen very quickly, we are already in the process of voting."
Russians will be able to buy the newly announced iPhone 14 even though Apple stopped selling its products in Russia after the invasion of Ukraine, a government minister has claimed.
“If consumers want to buy these phones, you’re welcome. They will have that chance,” Industry and Trade Minister Denis Manturov told Russia’s RIA Novosti news agency.
Apple gadgets have continued to arrive in Russia despite sanctions through the Kremlin’s “parallel imports” scheme, in which goods bought abroad are re-sold in Russia without permission from their manufacturers.

Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan has said grain from Russia should be exported too, and its president Vladimir Putin was right about grains exported from Ukraine under a UN-backed deal going to wealthy countries, not poor ones.
Speaking at a press conference with his Croatian counterpart, Mr Erdogan said Mr Putin was uncomfortable with these grains going to countries that sanction Russia.
On Wednesday, Mr Putin floated adding limits to Ukrainian grain exports
Secretary of State Antony Blinken has arrived in Kyiv on a surprise visit as the United States unveiled nearly $2.7 billion in new military support to Ukraine and neighbours to face Russia.
Mr Blinken travelled in secrecy on his second trip to Kyiv since the Russian invasion in February.
Tens of thousands of people in Belgorod, a south-western Russian city that served as the launchpad for the invasion of Ukraine, were left without electricity and water supply on Thursday after overnight explosions at a power distribution station, writes Nataliya Vasilyeva.
Footage broadcast on local media showed a series of explosions lighting up the station at around midnight.
Konstantin Polezhayev, deputy governor of Belgorod, said in a statement on Thursday that the blackout affected about a third of the city after the Yuzhnya power distribution station went offline due to what he described as a closed circuit.
Power supply to most of the residents was reportedly restored by noon, while photographs from the power station released by Mr Polezhayev’s office did not appear to show any significant damage.
Russian military infrastructure in Belgorod, near the Ukrainian border, has been targeted in numerous suspected Ukrainian attacks since the spring. Kyiv has not officially claimed responsibility for those attacks or Wednesday’s explosion in Belgorod.
The United States on Thursday announced $675 million in additional military equipment for Ukraine, as it said allies' efforts in bolstering Kyiv were now visibly paying off on the battlefield.
Hosting a new round of talks with partners in Germany, US Defence Secretary Lloyd Austin said Kyiv was now not only resisting Russian invaders, but is mounting a counter-offensive in the south.
"It's fitting that we're meeting back here at Ramstein," he said, referring to the US airbase in western Germany where the first of the "Ukraine Defence Contact Group" meetings on coordinating armaments support for Kyiv took place.
"Now, we're seeing the demonstrable success of our common efforts on the battlefield," he said, stressing that allies are in it "for the long haul".
The Baltic members of the European Union have agreed to coordinate a visa ban for most Russian citizens arriving at their borders, writes James Crisp.
Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania will aim to pass the measures, which go further than restrictions recently agreed at EU level, by mid-September and in the next ten days.
"It means Russians will not be able to cross the border," Latvian foreign minister Edgars Rinkevičius said, as his Estonia counterpart urged other countries to join the ban.
The countries, which border Russia,  will stop issuing new tourist visas but also reject visas granted to Russians by other EU member states in the bloc’s passport-free Schengen zone.
There will be exceptions for humanitarian reasons, lorry drivers and diplomats with full details to be released by the former Soviet Union countries in the coming days.
Finland, Denmark, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden did not join the ban after a meeting of Baltic and Nordic foreign ministers in Kaunas, Lithuania, on Wednesday.
The United Nations said there are "credible allegations" that Russian forces have forcibly removed children from Ukraine to Russia for adoption as part of larger-scale relocations and deportations.
Moscow has been accused of unlawfully detaining, interrogating and deporting up to 1.6 million Ukrainians, including 1,800 children.
"There have been credible allegations of forced transfers of unaccompanied children to Russian occupied territory, or to the Russian Federation itself," Ilze Brands Kehris, the assistant UN secretary-general for human rights, told the Security Council on Wednesday.
"We are concerned that the Russian authorities have adopted a simplified procedure to grant Russian citizenship to children without parental care, and that these children would be eligible for adoption by Russian families."
Russian forces were also placing Ukrainians in occupied territories through invasive security checks that have involved numerous human rights violations, Ms Ilze Brands Kehris said.
She said some Ukrainians judged as close to the Ukraine government or military have been tortured and forcibly removed and sent to Russian penal colonies and other detention centres.
Russian UN Ambassador Vasily Nebenzya has rebuffed the allegations, calling them "unfounded". He claimed Ukrainians were fleeing their country "to save themselves from the criminal regime".
The body of a British aid worker who was reported to have died while being detained by Russian-backed separatists in Ukraine shows signs of "possible unspeakable torture", Ukraine's foreign minister has said.
Paul Urey, 45, died in captivity in July, according to the human rights ombudsmanfor the Moscow-supported leadership in Donetsk.
Daria Morozova, the ombudsman, branded Mr Urey a "mercenary" and claimed he died in captivity of chronic illnesses and stress.
"From our side, he was given the necessary medical assistance despite the grave crimes he committed," she added.
However, Ukraine's foreign minister Dmytro Kuleba said on Wednesday Mr Urey's body had been returned "with signs of possible unspeakable torture".
About 280,000 tonnes of agricultural products will be exported in the near future from Ukrainian ports for the World Food Programme under a UN-brokered deal, the Ukrainian infrastructure ministry has said.
President Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday Russia and the developing world had been "cheated" by the deal and he wanted to revise the agreement as Ukrainian exports were not going to the world's poorest countries as originally intended.
Ukraine, however, says around 2.37 million tonnes of food have already left its Black Sea ports, including 1.04 million tonnes for Asian countries and 470,000 tonnes for African states.
Belarus has started military exercises by the city of Brest near the Polish border, its capital Minsk and the northeast region of Vitebsk, the defence ministry said on Thursday.
It said the exercises, which are set to last until September 14, will practice "liberating territory temporarily seized by the enemy" and regaining control over border regions.
According to the ministry, the level of troops and military equipment involved in the exercise did not require them to provide notice under OSCE guidelines.
Ukrainian forces recaptured at least two villages in a surprise offensive that broke through Russian front lines south of Kharkiv on Wednesday.
Ukrainian and Russian sources reported Ukraine had captured the settlements of Verbivka and Volokhiv Yar, and “operationally surrounded” the town of Balakliya.
The advances, which were not officially confirmed by either side, would put Ukrainian soldiers at least a dozen miles behind the Russian front line and position them to threaten a key supply line to the Russian forces in northern Donbas.
Ukraine’s army and government did not announce the assault that began near Balakliya on Tuesday, and have refused to comment on its progress or objectives.
Read the full story by Roland Oliphant here
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has declared next year's budget as a war budget, pledging more than a trillion hryvnias (£23.7 billion) to defence and security spending.
In an evening video address on Wednesday, Mr Zelensky said social obligations such as pensions had to be covered in full and non-critical expenses reduced as much as possible.
"It is clear that this will be the budget of a country at war," he said.
"More than a trillion hryvnias next year will go to the security and defense sector. This is going to be the number one priority."
Vladimir Putin has threatened to “freeze” Europe with a total shutdown of energy supplies if Brussels presses ahead with a price cap on Russian gas.
In a fiery speech delivered in Vladivostok, Russia’s president warned that Europeans would face a bleak winter if the Kremlin stopped deliveries to the Continent.
Speaking at an economic conference, he said: “We will not supply anything at all if it is contrary to our interests.
“No gas, no oil, no coal, no fuel oil, nothing.”
Read the full story here

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2022/09.title: The battle of Brixham is about much more than a fish market
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2022/09.subtitle: Yachties and fisherman are squaring up in Devon over plans to extend the town’s quay – and the fight is reflective of Britain today
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2022/09.text:
The clue to Brixham’s cultural identity is in the names of the bustling eateries jumbled along the quay: Brixham Fish, Claws Indoors, the Sprat and Mackerel pub. The smell of fish hangs, rich and tangy, in the Devon air. Beside the water lie the tools of the trade that has long formed the backbone of the local economy: heaps of nets, ropes, lobster pots and chains.
Here, the booming fishing industry rubs up against tourism. Holiday-makers weave their way between the fishing gear; they eat fish and chips on the wall overlooking the trawlers.
But a new proposal to extend Brixham’s fish quay and market – the largest in England by value of fish sold – threatens the equilibrium in this English Riviera town. Last month, Torbay Council announced it had submitted a bid to secure up to £20 million from the Government’s Levelling Up Fund, “to accelerate economic growth locally”. Under the plans, a new 2,250 sq m deck – about a quarter of a football pitch – would be created over the sea, accommodating a 2,000 sq m fish market, which would more than double its current capacity.
This development, says the council, could allow for an additional £20 million of catch to be processed each year, creating as many as 160 jobs and boosting the local economy to the tune of £38.5 million.
The market, run by Brixham Trawler Agents, already attracts buyers from across Europe, who bid remotely for catches landed not only in Brixham but in ports across England and Wales and brought to Brixham by road. Last year, a record-breaking £43.6 million of fish was sold here.
Increasing the market’s capacity could no doubt be seen as within the spirit of the Britain of the Brexiteers’ dreams. And Torbay, the council area in which Brixham sits, voted clearly in favour of leaving the European Union.
Except that there are rumbles of discontent; doubts about what the extension will really mean. From yachting enthusiasts to day boat and small boat skippers to environmental activists, there runs a strong current of opposition. “The idea that expanding the market creates jobs is a myth,” says Richard Spreckley, commodore of Brixham Yacht Club, which fears the loss of some of its moorings as a result of the scheme. “All it does is increase space for transport or for boxes of fish.” So it won’t help level up the town? “Absolutely not. It’s simply writing cheques for people who have a lot of money already.”
These people, say opponents of the scheme, are those who profit from the activity of the trawlers, as well as those who truck fish caught elsewhere into the town to be sold at its successful online fish auction.
More than 40 species are landed, the main catches being lemon and Dover sole, squid, monkfish, turbot and cuttlefish – known as black gold. It is a lucrative business, a success story: Brixham’s fish market has survived the extra administrative costs created by Brexit and managed to thrive.
Yet not everyone here is thriving. As Torbay Council says, the wider area is “recognised as being left behind”. About 15 per cent of residents live in areas ranked among the 20 per cent most deprived in England in relation to living environment. The town also has a higher than average rate of Universal Credit claimants (10.7 per cent of the population, compared with the English average of 10.3 per cent).
But the older fishermen claim that when it comes to their occupation, “as a generation, the young lads aren’t willing to do the work”. Skipper George Stevens says the boats depend on foreign nationals to make up their crew numbers. “The work ethic of the Filipino lads is second to none,” he says. Brixham’s fishing tradition dates back to the 1300s, and Parliament first approved the construction of its fish market in 1799. By 1850 the town had become the largest fishery in England, a position it subsequently lost and then, by 2000, had regained.
The problem, say environmentalists, is it’s not sustainable and should not be the focus of the council’s bid for levelling up funding – which also includes plans for a new electronics and photonics production park.
Jim Funnell, an eco-activist and founder of Better Devon, says the beam trawlers that fish at Brixham by pulling heavy-duty nets across the seabed damage marine habitats and release large amounts of carbon. “Devastating the seas and destroying the livelihoods of other sustainable fishers and fisheries through industrial fishing should not be encouraged,” he writes in his objection to the project.
Fish stocks are declining, he points out. “So why are we spending valuable money on expanding fish processing capacity? In no other industry or sector would you invest millions in a product that is getting harder to source and so tightly regulated.”
If the image of Brixham’s fishery is one of “quaint heritage”, the likelihood is the council’s plan “will encourage Brixham to become the hub of industrial fishing activity”, he warns. “There’s lots of festering discontent with the way the fishing industry always gets the focus. This application is going to benefit purely an industry that’s already reaping huge profits.” The smaller, more sustainable fishers “constantly get squeezed out”, he adds.
Tensions boiled over in May, when members of Extinction Rebellion staged a protest in Brixham against “industrial” fishing methods and the proposed use of public money to extend the market rather than focusing on other priorities.
“Brixham desperately needs regeneration and social housing,” says Spreckley. He would also like to see more moorings to cater to those who want to use the water for yachting. The yacht club, formed in 1937, has 700 members. “There’s a huge demand for moorings,” he says.
It is, perhaps, a microcosm of a wider conflict: on one hand, the idea that we should invest in new infrastructure to boost growth or build more homes to reduce the housing shortage; on the other, the local interests that are often stacked against development, the environmental concerns, and the desire to preserve rather than expand. Reconciling these conflicting imperatives is seldom easy.
But Torbay Council, which expects to learn the outcome of its bid this autumn, says the project would bring benefits. “If successful, this funding will support the growth of the fish processing sector, as opposed to the fish catching sector – which is linked to environmental issues of concern,” says a spokesman. “Furthermore, this project will not lead to more fish being caught as the UK quota sets a fish catch limit for the country … By increasing the fish processing capacity, Brixham will be able to receive fish transportation lorries that are fuller than they are currently operating at.”
Indeed, Brixham’s fishing business has “substantial growth potential which Torbay needs to capitalise on”, Councillor Swithin Long, cabinet member for economic regeneration, tourism and housing, has stressed. “These projects will create new, higher value jobs and will drive international trade, playing a huge part in levelling up the local economy and bringing positive change for our communities.”
In the harbour, a firm called Ecomotus is adapting vessels to release fewer carbon emissions and reduce fuel costs, using hydrogen. From up on the hill, where the yacht club is situated, the plump shadows of fish can be seen darting through the waters below as another trawler glides, slowly and silently, out to sea.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2022/09.title: Just Stop Oil ‘sorry’ for leaving plastic rubbish near protest site on farm
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2022/09.subtitle: Charles Goadby, a farmer in Warwickshire, accused the group of hypocrisy given their action on the environment
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2022/09.text:
Campaign group Just Stop Oil have apologised for leaving plastic rubbish near a protest site on a farm, prompting accusations of hypocrisy.
Charles Goadby, a farmer, said he had found a pile of plastic bottles, chairs and other rubbish near a tunnel dug by a group of protesters in an effort to block the Kingsbury Oil Terminal in Warwickshire.
Mr Goadby accused the group of “destroying the countryside and putting our wildlife at risk with rubbish” in a video on Twitter.
“What I want to know from somebody senior at Just Stop Oil is, how is this acceptable?” he said. “How can you justify this?”
He also said the dumping of the rubbish was hypocritical given their action on the environment.
“What amazed me was in the rubbish there were loads of the non recyclable coffee cups and lids and loads of plastic bottles of water, still wrapped (so not being reused) and all from a brand that’s shipped from France,” he said. “Have an argument and stand up for what you believe by all means, but at least be consistent!”
In a statement in response, Just Stop Oil said Mr Goadby was “right to be angry”.
“Just Stop Oil is sorry that the site was not cleaned up, this is now being organised. The area should have been cleaned, so that the land, people and wildlife are protected,” it said.
The group added that the rubbish had been deposited by police after they cleared the tunnel when protesters were forcibly removed and arrested.
Around 50 campaigners were arrested at the site a week ago, when they blocked oil tankers entering and leaving the oil terminal for around four and a half hours.
The protest group, which wants the immediate end to licensing for the exploration, development and production of oil and gas in the UK, said the dumping of rubbish did not compare to the environmental destruction of fossil fuels.
“If you are more outraged and furious about this small mess than you are about the threat to land, people and wildlife posed by the climate crisis then you need to think again,” it said in a statement. “The damage that is coming, aided and supported by our government can not be picked up and taken away.”
Five of the protesters on Tuesday walked free from court, after admitting to breaching an injunction against blocking the oil terminal, which also stopped a worker getting to a medical appointment.
The protesters were accused of “stretching” the resources of police dealing with the Queen’s funeral by Judge Emma Kelly at Birmingham Crown Court.
The judge jailed each of the protesters for 23 days, but suspended the terms for two years, because it was their "first breach".
Sentencing them, she said: "Your actions caused significant harm to policing in Warwickshire when resources were already stretched to capacity by the Queen's death.
"Simply because of the sheer number of you who had chosen to gather in one place, it created a risk of clearly significant harm should police be needed elsewhere."

image.caption: The rubbish was found near a tunnel dug by a group of protesters trying to block the Kingsbury Oil Terminal in Warwickshire
Mr Goady was not best pleased to find a pile of plastic bottles, chairs and other rubbish
